funeral of slain Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Ibrahim Raisi, the spokesperson for
Iran's Parliament National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, warned that Tehran could
reconsider its nuclear commitments after Israel's defense minister, Israel Kats, threatened to
assassinate Mujtaba Khamenei. In an ex-post, Raisi said, and I quote,
one of Iran's options in the event of another attack could be 90% enrichment. We will review
it in the parliament. A procession passed by the coffins of Iran's slain supreme leader,
Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and his family on Friday. State media was quoted by the Associated Press as
saying, On Friday morning, security forces carried Khamenei's coffin overhead by hand as it arrived
at the Grand Musala in Tehran. Religious leaders walked past Khamenei's coffin as well as others
of his slain family, including his 14-month-old granddaughter, Zahra Mohammadi Golpayagani.
According to state media, Khamenei's mortal remains sat within a coffin on a stage with red tulips in
front of it. Beginning Saturday, Iran will hold a day-long funeral for Khamenei and his body will
be transported to cities in both Iran and neighboring Iraq.
The Middle East is once again on edge. As Iran prepares for one of the most significant state
funerals in its modern history, a stark warning has been issued to the United States and Israel.
A senior Iranian military commander has declared that any attack on the country during this sensitive
period would trigger what he described as a harsh retaliation from Iran's armed forces.
Commander Ali Abdalahi said, and I quote, We warn the enemies of Iran, especially the U.S.
and the Zionist regime, to avoid any miscalculation and to think about the harsh retaliation our armed
forces would make to any threat and aggression against our country.
The warning comes as millions are expected to mourn the late supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali
Khamenei, who was killed in airstrikes on the opening day of the war.
Funeral ceremonies are set to begin on July 4th in Tehran, before continuing through several
cities ending with his burial in his hometown of Mashhad on July 9th.
The latest threat follows remarks by Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, who reportedly
said Iran's current supreme leader, Mochtaba Khamenei, was marked for death, comments that
have further inflamed already soaring tensions.
Iran says any threat against its leadership or its people will be met with an immediate
and decisive response.
Meanwhile, security has been tightened across the country.
Authorities are imposing temporary airspace restrictions over Tehran, Mashhad and other
major cities as preparations intensify.
With emotions running high and military rhetoric escalating on both sides, the region now braces
for what could become another dangerous flashpoint in an already volatile conflict.
A fresh standoff has erupted over Iran's nuclear program as Tehran flatly rejects international
inspections of nuclear facilities bombed by the United States, setting the stage for another
major confrontation with the UN's nuclear watchdog.
Iran has ruled out allowing inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency, or IAEA,
to visit key nuclear facilities struck during recent US military operations, escalating tensions
over the future of Tehran's nuclear program.
Iran's chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagheer-Ghalibov, dismissed reports suggesting
the UN nuclear watchdog would be granted access to the bombed sites, calling those claims completely
false during an appearance on Iranian state television.
According to Golibov, IAEA inspectors have no right to inspect nuclear facilities targeted
by US strikes, including the strategically important Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan nuclear sites, all of
which remain at the centre of international concern.
The senior Iranian official insisted that IAEA access remains limited to only two locations, the
Boucher nuclear power plant and the Tehran research reactor, signalling that Tehran has no intention
of opening its damaged nuclear infrastructure to international inspectors.
The remarks directly contradict recent comments from IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi, who
said existing agreements require inspectors to verify conditions on the ground, and stressed
that the agency must eventually gain access to the relevant facilities.
